content: Tinidazole is metabolized by the hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. The following interactions and precautions should be noted: 1. Ticagrelor: This drug increases the level or effect of tinidazole by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor the patient closely. 2. Ticlopidine: Similar to ticagrelor, ticlopidine also increases tinidazole levels or effects via CYP3A4 inhibition. Exercise caution and monitor closely. 3. Tipranavir: This drug elevates tinidazole levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Close monitoring is required. 4. Tisagenlecleucel: Tinidazole and tisagenlecleucel can mutually enhance each other's immunosuppressive effects, increasing the risk of infection. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 5. Tranylcypromine: This drug increases tinidazole levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4. Use caution and monitor closely. 6. Trazodone: Trazodone also increases tinidazole levels or effects via CYP3A4 inhibition. Monitor the patient closely. 7. Tucatinib: Tucatinib significantly increases tinidazole levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4. Avoid concurrent use or use an alternative drug. If unavoidable, reduce the dose of the CYP3A substrate as per product labeling and monitor closely. 8. Valproic Acid: This drug increases tinidazole levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Verapamil: Verapamil elevates tinidazole levels or effects via CYP3A4 inhibition. Close monitoring is necessary. 10. Vinblastine, Vincristine, Vinorelbine: These drugs increase tinidazole levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 11. Voriconazole: Voriconazole increases tinidazole levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4. Monitor the patient closely. 12. Zafirlukast: This drug increases tinidazole levels or effects via CYP3A4 inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 13. Zileuton: Zileuton elevates tinidazole levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4. Close monitoring is required. 14. Ziprasidone: This drug increases tinidazole levels or effects via CYP3A4 inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. Adverse Effects: Common side effects include anorexia (2-3%), constipation (<1%), dizziness (<1%), dysgeusia (4-6%), dyspepsia (1-2%), headache (<1%), nausea (3-5%), vomiting (1-2%), and weakness/fatigue/malaise (1-2%). Rare but serious side effects include ataxia, Candida overgrowth, convulsions, transient peripheral neuropathy, numbness, paresthesia, diarrhea, darkened urine, tongue discoloration, transient leukopenia/neutropenia, and severe irreversible hepatotoxicity or acute liver failure (notably in patients with Cockayne syndrome). Carcinogenicity has been observed in mice and rats treated chronically with metronidazole, a structurally related nitroimidazole drug. While such data are not reported for tinidazole, the structural similarity warrants caution. Limit use to approved indications and avoid chronic use. Contraindications and Warnings: Tinidazole is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity, during the first trimester of pregnancy, and in those with Cockayne syndrome due to the risk of severe hepatotoxicity. Caution is advised in patients with a history of blood dyscrasias or hepatic impairment. Convulsive seizures and peripheral neuropathy (characterized by numbness or paresthesia) have been reported. Discontinue therapy promptly if abnormal neurologic signs appear. Prescribing tinidazole in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is discouraged, as it increases the risk of drug-resistant bacteria. Prolonged treatment may lead to bacterial overgrowth or Candida vaginitis when used for bacterial vaginosis. Pregnancy and Lactation: Limited data from case-control studies and case reports in pregnant women are insufficient to determine the risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Untreated lower genital tract infections during pregnancy pose risks. Tinidazole is present in human milk, but no adverse effects on breastfed infants or milk production have been reported. However, due to the potential for serious adverse reactions, including tumorigenicity, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for 72 hours after the last dose. Nursing mothers may pump and discard milk during this period to minimize infant exposure. Pharmacokinetics: Tinidazole undergoes oxidation, hydroxylation, and conjugation. It is primarily excreted in urine (20-25% as unchanged drug) and feces (12%). Additional Notes: Use tinidazole only for approved indications and avoid chronic use. Safety and efficacy in pediatric patients under 3 years of age have not been established. The above information is for general educational purposes. Always consult the applicable plan provider for the most current formulary information.
